# neatHack Rules We Follow

Five rules can get the entry disqualified or cost it points. Each one has a control in the repo layout, so nobody has to remember it.

Atharva is working solo. Dates and availability are flexible. The rules stay fixed.

## Three Things Wait Until 12:30 PM IST on Oct 10

Checked at 9:59 IST on 2026-10-10: `firstrun` had 0 commits and only a `.gitignore`. Entire was off, and the GitHub repo did not exist.

1. Never open Claude Code inside `D:\Atharva\firstrun` before kickoff. Entire timestamps every session it records.
2. Never run `entire enable` before kickoff.
3. Never create the GitHub repo `HighnessAtharva/firstrun` before kickoff.

Allowed before kickoff, and already done: the folder, `git init`, the `plan/` junction, `.gitignore`, the Python 3.11 `.venv` with packages, and vendor-example spikes in `neathack-prep`.

## F1: No FirstRun Code Exists Before Sat Oct 10, 12:30 PM IST

The FAQ says: "You can plan your idea in advance, but all code must be written between the start on October 10 and the deadline on October 12. Finished or half-built projects cannot be brought into the event."

**The control:** three repos, each with one job.

| Repo | Visibility | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `D:\Atharva\NOTES` vault | private | This plan and the research. No code. |
| `D:\Atharva\neathack-prep` | private | Tool-learning spikes and setup notes. No FirstRun code. Never submitted. |
| `firstrun` | public | All FirstRun code, written fresh after kickoff. Created after 12:30 PM IST on Oct 10. |

**Allowed before kickoff:**

- Accounts, installs, keys, Docker in WSL.
- The plan, the spec in prose, the prompts, the list of test quickstarts, the video script.
- Running each vendor's own quickstart example in `neathack-prep/spikes/<tool>/` to learn the tool.
- Asking the organizers in Discord what counts as planning.

**Not allowed:**

- Writing any FirstRun logic before kickoff, in any repo.
- Copying anything from `spikes/` into `firstrun`.
- Building in a private repo and swapping in a clean public one.

**Be open about it:** the first entry in `firstrun/hackathon.md` says "Planning and tool tests happened before the event in a private repo. No FirstRun code was written before kickoff."

## F3: Entire Sees Only Sessions That Start After Kickoff

The Entire judging tool excludes work that starts before the event (`predates_event`). It also counts `entire` commands that the coding agent runs (`cli_awareness`).

**The control:**

1. Never run `entire enable` in `neathack-prep` or in the vault.
2. Practice Entire before kickoff only in a throwaway folder that you delete afterward, such as `D:\Atharva\entire-sandbox`.
3. Create `firstrun` after 12:30 PM IST on Oct 10. Run `entire enable --agent claude-code --search-skill --agent-help-skill` before its first commit.
4. Let Claude Code run the `entire` commands, such as `entire status` and `entire checkpoint list`, so they land in the session transcript.
5. On Monday, run the Entire jury tool on `firstrun` with the real start time. It must report no excluded work.

## F2: The Video Covers Five Points for Each of the Three Tools

The video is 3 minutes or less. For each of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai it shows architecture, implementation, runtime, reasoning and result. The script in `06 Demo and Submission.md` names all 15 points.

## F5: No Cut Ever Removes a Use of the Three Required Tools

The FAQ says every project must use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, "with a clear role for each", and the demo must cover all three. That is 25% of the score, and a missing tool can cost the entry. The simplicity tests in `01 Project Plan.md` apply to FirstRun's own features only. They never apply to the tools.

**Each day leaves evidence for all three tools.** Check the boxes at the end of the day:

| Day | neatlogs | Entire | cfo.ai |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sat | [ ] Every FirstRun run is a trace. [ ] 3 `v1` traces exist. | [ ] `entire enable` before commit 1. [ ] Every commit has an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer. [ ] Graph set up. [ ] Trails turned on, Layer 1 Trail created. | [x] Signed up through `cfo.ai/neathacks`, then cancelled in Billing (done 2026-10-10). |
| Sun | [ ] 2 or more detections. [ ] 1 Investigate. [ ] The fix pulled in over MCP. [ ] 3 `v2` traces. [ ] The before and after table. [ ] 1 failed-and-recovered trace. [ ] 1 eval. | [ ] Layer 2 Trail. [ ] Brain set up. [ ] `entire graph stats` number saved. | [ ] Cost per run read from neatlogs, ready for the model. |
| Mon | [ ] Trace links or screenshots in `evidence/`. | [ ] Checkpoint link plus its ID in the README. [ ] `evidence/graph.ndjson`. [ ] Jury self-test run. | [ ] The plan with pricing, costs, revenue and runway. [ ] Share link, `.xlsx` and `BUSINESS_PLAN.md` in the repo. |
| Video | [ ] 5 points, 40 seconds | [ ] 5 points, 30 seconds | [ ] 5 points, 30 seconds |

**The rule for a slipping day:** cut a FirstRun feature before you cut any box in this table. If time runs out, the agent can do less. The tool evidence still has to be complete.

## F4: Submit at 7:00 PM IST Sharp on Mon Oct 12 to Land in the First 50

- The window opens at 7:00 PM IST and closes at 11:55 PM IST. Late posts are not judged.
- neatlogs and cfo.ai engage with the **first 50 quote posts only**. Post 51 falls outside that promise. Their engagement likely helps the 15% build-in-public score and the $500 community award.
- So the post goes live between 7:00 and 7:05 PM IST.

**The control:**

3. At 6:55 PM, open https://neatlogs.com/hackathon and refresh until the **Submit on X** button shows.
4. At 7:00 PM, click it, paste the text, keep the official post attached, and publish. Opening the draft alone does not submit.

If the work is not finished at 7:00 PM, submit at 7:00 PM anyway. The repo can still take commits until 11:55 PM, because code may be written up to the deadline. The video link in the post cannot change, so finish the video first.

# FirstRun: The Agent That Does Your Quickstart Before Your Users Do

FirstRun reads a dev tool's quickstart page, runs every step in a clean container like a brand-new developer, and stops only when the last step works. When a step breaks, it finds the cause, patches the docs, proves the patch in a second clean run, and opens a pull request.

One line for the video: **"Your quickstart broke last Tuesday. Your users found out first. FirstRun finds out first now."**

## The Simple Version Wins, and Every Feature Must Pass Three Tests

The judges see about 100 projects. The one they remember can be said in one breath and shown in one minute. Every feature passes three tests, or it waits until after the event:

1. **Explain test.** It fits the one-sentence pitch below without a second sentence.
2. **Demo test.** It shows up on screen in the 60-second run below.
3. **Score test.** A judging category or an evidence item needs it.

**The pitch, one sentence:** "FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run."

**The whole product is one command:**

```bash
firstrun run https://docs.example.com/quickstart
```

**The output is one screen, three lines that matter:**

```text
✗ step 3/6  pip install chromadb==0.3   ->  No matching distribution
✓ fixed     docs bug: pin removed, patched step 3
✓ verified  fresh container, 6/6 steps pass, 94 s, $0.04
```

Those three lines are a design target, not a result. The numbers on them come from the real run on the day.

**The 60-second demo follows that order:** red step, the agent's reason, green verified, the drafted PR. Then one click into the neatlogs trace that shows the same run as spans.

**The three words of the story:** break, fix, prove. The video, the README and every post use these three words.

**Cut, because each fails at least one test:**

| Feature | Fails | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|
| Layer 3, the parallel coordinator | Explain test: it needs a second sentence | After the event |
| AWS nightly runner | Demo test: nothing visible in 60 seconds | Say "runs nightly" only as the product plan in cfo.ai |
| Crustdata owner lookup | Score test: no category needs it | After the event |
| A web UI or a static HTML report page | Demo test: the terminal plus neatlogs already show it | After the event, unless Chetan says the terminal confuses judges |
| 5 demo targets | Demo test: 3 tell the same story faster | Keep 3: the neatlogs quickstart, one real or fixture break, FirstRun's own README |

**The three tests never touch the required tools.** neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai are mandatory, so rule F5 in `07 Rules We Follow.md` protects every use of them. The tests cut FirstRun features only.

**Kept, because each passes all three:** the planner, the clean container, recovery with ask-once, the verification run, the drafted PR, neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints and Trails, and the cfo.ai plan.

**The Entire checkpoint-in-PR idea stays a stretch.** It passes the explain test only as "and every PR links the agent session that wrote it". Build it only after the 60-second demo works end to end.

## The Problem Is Silent Docs Rot

- A quickstart breaks when a package gets renamed, a flag gets removed or a version moves. Nobody on the team gets an alert.
- The first person who finds the break is a new user. Most new users leave instead of filing an issue.
- DevRel teams track "time to first success", but nobody measures it every night.

You run DevRel at AccuKnox. You write docs and quickstarts. This problem is yours, so the pitch is honest and you can talk about it without notes.

## Why This Idea Beats the Other Two

| Option | One-line verdict |
|---|---|
| **O1 FirstRun (pick this)** | Every judge works at a dev-tool company and owns docs or onboarding. Clear value, easy to demo, hits all 8 focus areas. |
| O2 Trace Medic: an agent that reads neatlogs traces of another agent and ships the fix | Maximum neatlogs use, but it copies neatlogs' own product. Many teams will build it. |
| O3 Claim Court: an agent that fact-checks a technical blog post with sources | Fits your writing system, but research agents are common and the demo is less visual. |

Your Jeff bookshelf cannot be the entry, because all code must be written during the event. Its Jev ranking idea lives on inside FirstRun as the failure classifier.

## The Last Winner Tested Docs Too, and FirstRun Must Look Different

At Syndicate by Maximor (Sep 5 to 6, co-hosted by neatlogs), Prateek Karnal and Ajay Yadav judged. First place went to **Skeptic**, an agent that tested its own tools' docs, found 12 of 12 documented promises broken, and published a corrected `TOOLS.md`. Second place, **Loop**, showed task success going from 0% to 100% across 3 runs.

This proves two judges reward docs testing. It also means FirstRun must look different from Skeptic in the first 15 seconds of the video:

- Skeptic tested the docs of the tools inside its own agent. FirstRun tests public quickstarts of real products, end to end, in a real container.
- Skeptic published a corrected file. FirstRun opens a PR on the real project.
- Copy what made both winners win: real before and after numbers, an honest null result when one happens, and one narrow problem.

Name Skeptic only if a judge asks. Show the difference instead of claiming it.

## How FirstRun Covers All 8 Focus Areas

The judges score "the agent" against these eight areas. FirstRun hits each one by design, not as an add-on.

| Focus area | What FirstRun does |
|---|---|
| Planning | Turns the docs page into an ordered runbook: each step, its command, and the result it expects. |
| Tool use | Firecrawl reads the docs. A shell runs inside a Docker container. GitHub opens the PR. |
| State | Writes a checkpoint after every step, so a crashed run resumes at the step it reached. |
| Context | Loads only the quickstart page and the pages it links to, never the whole docs site. |
| Execution | Keeps going until the last step passes or the retry budget runs out. |
| Recovery | On a failed step it classifies the cause, searches for the fix, patches, and retries. |
| Verification | Re-runs the patched runbook in a fresh container with no improvising allowed. Only a pass counts. |
| Iteration | Each step's real output decides the next action. |

## The Agent Asks a Human Once, Then Reuses the Answer

Ajay Yadav, the neatlogs founder, wrote "Self-healing is self-defeating" on 30 Sep. His fix is "ask just once": the agent asks a human on a new judgment call, saves the answer, and reuses it.

FirstRun builds that in. When it cannot tell whether a failure is a docs bug or intended behavior, it asks you once in the terminal. It stores your answer in `precedents.json` and never asks that question again. Jev makes the call and returns a probability, so FirstRun asks only when the probability sits below 0.7.

## Each Tool Gets One Clear Job

The FAQ says each tool needs "a clear role", and the video must cover all three.

| Tool | Its job in FirstRun | The proof judges can check |
|---|---|---|
| **neatlogs** | Traces every run. Detections flag bad runs. Investigate finds why the agent itself failed. The fix comes into Claude Code over the neatlogs MCP. | Two traces, before and after, with a numbers table. One trace of a failed step and the recovery. |
| **Entire** | Records every Claude Code session behind every commit, from commit 1. `entire why` shows the prompt behind any line. entire-graph maps the repo. | `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers on every commit, the entire.io commit view, and `graph.ndjson` in the repo. |
| **cfo.ai** | Plans the business with real numbers. The cost per run comes from neatlogs, not from a guess. | A read-only cfo.ai Page link plus the `.xlsx` export, with pricing, costs, revenue and runway. |

The neatlogs-to-cfo.ai link is the move most teams will miss. neatlogs measures what one run costs, and cfo.ai builds the pricing on that measured cost. Say this sentence in the video.

## The Stack Uses Python and Your Own Tools

- **Language:** Python, because neatlogs auto-instruments Python and TypeScript has no auto-instrumentation.
- **Agent:** Claude Agent SDK (Python). neatlogs turns each `query()` into an AGENT span, with one LLM span per turn and one TOOL span per tool call.
- **Sandbox:** Docker Engine inside your WSL Ubuntu. One fresh container per run.
- **Docs reader:** Firecrawl CLI, which you already have.
- **Judgment calls:** Jev, the TypeSafe model, called with new code written during the event. Read `D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\jev\jev.py` for the API shape, but do not copy the file, because all code must be new. It classifies each failure as docs bug, environment, product bug or needs a secret, with a probability.
- **Optional, only if time remains:** AWS credits to run nightly, and the Crustdata 5,000 free credits to find who owns each docs site.

## The Scope Is Three Layers, and Only Layer 1 Is Mandatory

Build in this order. Stop adding layers at 2:00 PM IST on Monday, whatever is done.

1. **Layer 1, must ship (Saturday):** one quickstart URL in, a runbook out, every step run in Docker, a report out, every run traced in neatlogs.
2. **Layer 2, should ship (Sunday):** recovery, a clean verification re-run, the ask-once precedent store, a docs patch and a PR.
3. **Layer 3, nice to have (Sunday night):** a coordinator that runs 5 quickstarts in parallel, one worker each, then merges the reports. Prateek Karnal builds parallel agent fleets, so he will notice this.

## Five Test Quickstarts Follow Four Rules

Pick them on Friday. Picking is planning, so it is allowed before kickoff.

1. The quickstart is public and runs on Linux in a container.
2. It needs no paid account. A free API key that you add to the container is fine.
3. It has 10 steps or fewer, so one run finishes in minutes.
4. The tool is known to developers, so a found break gets attention.

Two slots are already filled:

- **The neatlogs Python quickstart.** The judges see their own docs pass or fail. Either result helps them.
- **FirstRun's own README, as the last run on Monday.** Haimantika Mitra owns docs at Entire and will look for a README that reproduces. Proving it with your own agent is the closing shot of the video.

## The Before and After Story Is Planned, Not Hoped For

The judges want two traces and a numbers table. Plan the story on purpose.

1. **Before (Saturday night):** run v1 on 5 quickstarts. v1 will fail in ways you can see, such as looping on a failed command or inventing a flag.
2. **Find the cause:** a neatlogs detection flags the bad runs. Run Investigate on them. All paid neatlogs plans are free during neatHack (organizer email, 2026-10-10), so Investigate has no monthly cap.
3. **Fix:** pull the neatlogs fix into Claude Code over MCP. Commit it, so Entire records the session.
4. **After (Sunday):** run the same 5 quickstarts. Fill the table below from the neatlogs CLI.

| Metric | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Quickstarts finished | ? of 5 | ? of 5 |
| Average tool calls per run | ? | ? |
| Average cost per run | ? | ? |
| Average time per run | ? | ? |
| Failed steps recovered | ? | ? |

Never invent a number in this table. Fill it from `neatlogs analytics kpis` and `neatlogs analytics cost`.

## The Business Plan Rests on Measured Cost

Build this in cfo.ai on Monday morning. Every figure below is a starting assumption for Ari. Replace each one with a measured number.

- **Who pays:** DevRel and docs teams at dev-tool companies.
- **Pricing to test:** Free for 1 quickstart run weekly. Team at $49 a month for 10 quickstarts nightly. Scale at $299 a month for 100 quickstarts and PRs.
- **Cost per run:** the measured neatlogs cost per run, plus container compute.
- **Scenarios:** Base and Growth, the same two the hackathon page shows.
- **Runway:** a solo founder with no salary, so runway is the months until revenue covers model cost.

## Five Risks Have a Plan Already

| Risk | Plan |
|---|---|
| R1 Docker setup eats Saturday | Install Docker in WSL on Friday. Setup is not project code. |
| R2 cfo.ai access approval is slow | Request access tonight. |
| R4 The Entire judge reads a different checkpoint store | Ask in Discord on Friday. If nobody answers, run `entire enable --checkpoint-backend branch`. |
| R5 Every chosen quickstart passes | A pass is still a result, for example "5 of 5 pass", with the measured time to first success for each. Also keep one older docs version as a labeled test fixture that is known to break. |
| R7 A real company's docs look bad in public | Open a polite issue or PR first. Post about it after. Never mock a team. |

# FirstRun Spec

This spec is planning, written in prose before kickoff, as the rules allow. It holds no code. At kickoff, Claude Code builds from it through the prompts in `05 Kickoff Prompts.md`. Every decision here is made once, so Saturday goes to building.

## FirstRun Takes One URL and Returns a Verdict With Proof

- **Input:** the URL of a quickstart page, or a file `targets.txt` with one URL per line.
- **Output per run**, in `runs/<run_id>/`:
  - `report.md`: pass or fail, the first failed step, the cause, the fix, time to first success, cost.
  - `runbook.json`: the steps as the planner read them.
  - `state.json`: the checkpoint after each step.
  - `patch.diff`: the docs change, only when a docs bug was found and verified.
  - `pr_body.md`: a draft PR text, only with a verified patch.
- **The user:** a DevRel or docs engineer who wants to know their quickstart works before a new user tries it.

## The Command Line Has Four Commands

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `firstrun run <url>` | One full run on one quickstart |
| `firstrun run --targets targets.txt` | One run per line, one after another. |
| `firstrun run <url> --resume <run_id>` | Continue a crashed run from the last good step |
| `firstrun report` | A summary table across every run in `runs/` |

## A Runbook Step Has Six Fields

The planner turns the docs page into a list of steps. Each step has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | Step number, starting at 1 |
| `intent` | One plain sentence: what this step is for, such as "install the SDK" |
| `command` | The exact shell command from the docs, unchanged |
| `files` | Files the docs tell the user to create, with their content |
| `expected` | What success looks like: exit code 0, a line of output, a file that exists |
| `source_line` | Where in the docs page this step came from, so a patch can point at it |

The planner copies commands exactly. It never fixes a command while planning. Fixing happens only in recovery, where it is logged.

## The Model Is Fixed at Sonnet 5.5, Medium Effort

- Every model call in FirstRun uses `claude-sonnet-5-5` at medium effort. One constant sets both, and no other file names a model.
- Auth is `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, so calls draw on the Claude subscription. There is no Anthropic API key, and AWS Bedrock is not available on the hackathon account.
- Jev handles failure classification and is not an Anthropic call.
- Cost per run is the token count from neatlogs times the Sonnet 5.5 list price. Every report and the cfo.ai plan label it "list price, not billed".

## Each Step Moves Through Six States

`pending` → `running` → `passed`, or `running` → `failed` → `recovering` → `passed` (with a patch) or `gave_up`.

After the last step, the whole run moves to `verifying`, then to `verified` or `unverified`.

## Four Failure Classes Decide the Next Action

When a step fails, Jev classifies the error output into one class and returns a probability for each class.

| Class | Example | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| `docs_bug` | Package renamed, flag removed, wrong import path | Search for the fix, patch the step, retry |
| `environment` | Missing system package in the base image, network timeout | Fix the container, not the docs. Retry. Do not count it as a docs bug. |
| `product_bug` | The tool itself crashes on a correct command | Stop. Report it as a product bug. No docs patch. |
| `needs_secret` | The step asks for an API key the container lacks | Use a test key from the allowlist if one exists. Otherwise stop and report. |

**Ask once.** If the top probability is below 0.7, FirstRun asks the user in the terminal: "Is this a docs bug, an environment issue, a product bug, or a missing secret?" It stores the answer in `precedents.json`, keyed by a short signature of the error, and reuses it without asking again.

## Recovery Has a Hard Budget

The budget protects against the agent looping, which is the most common agent failure the neatlogs judges look for.

| Limit | Value | When it trips |
|---|---|---|
| Attempts per step | 3 | The step is marked `gave_up` |
| Tool calls per run | 25 | The run stops and reports |
| Cost per run | $0.50 | The run stops and reports |
| Time per step | 5 minutes | The command is killed |

Each limit check is a `GUARDRAIL` span in neatlogs, so a tripped limit is visible in the trace.

## Verification Allows No Improvising

A run counts as `verified` only when all three are true:

1. A brand-new container runs the runbook with every patch applied.
2. No model call happens during the verification run. Only the stored commands run.
3. Every step meets its `expected` result.

Verification is what turns "the agent says it works" into "it works". Say that sentence in the video.

## Neatlogs Sees Every Part of a Run

| Part of FirstRun | Span kind | Span name |
|---|---|---|
| One whole run | `WORKFLOW` | `firstrun.run` |
| Reading the docs page | `TOOL` | `read_docs` |
| Planning the runbook | `AGENT` | `planner` |
| Running one step | `TOOL` | `step.<id>` |
| Classifying a failure | `TOOL` | `classify_failure` |
| Recovery for one step | `AGENT` | `recover.<id>` |
| A budget check | `GUARDRAIL` | `budget` |
| The verification run | `GUARDRAIL` | `verify` |

**Tags:** `v1` for the first version, `v2` after the fix. **Metadata on every run:** `target` (the tool name), `run_id`, `variant`.

**Detections to create on Sunday morning,** in the neatlogs dashboard:

1. Condition: `tool_call_count > 25`, which catches a looping agent.
2. Condition: `cost_usd > 0.50`, which catches a run over budget.
3. Regex on step output: `command not found|No module named|unrecognized arguments`, which catches the most common docs breaks.

**Eval:** one human eval question per run, "Is the docs patch correct?", plus one AI evaluator that scores whether `report.md` names the real failed step. Paid plans are free during neatHack, so the AI evaluator costs nothing.

## The Container Is the Safety Boundary

- One fresh container per run, removed after the run.
- No folder from your PC is mounted into the container.
- Network access stays on, because quickstarts install packages.
- The only secrets in the container are test keys from an allowlist file that never enters git.
- FirstRun never opens a PR on another project by itself. It writes `pr_body.md`, and you open the PR by hand after you read it.

## Each Layer Has a Definition of Done

**Layer 1 is done when:**

- `firstrun run <neatlogs quickstart URL>` finishes and writes `report.md`.
- The run shows in neatlogs as one trace, with a `TOOL` span per step.
- A test with a saved docs page passes with no network.

**Layer 2 is done when:**

- A known-broken fixture fails on a step, gets classified, gets patched, and ends `verified`.
- A second run with the same error asks no question, because the precedent exists.
- `patch.diff` and `pr_body.md` exist for the fixture.

**Layer 3 is cut** (see the three tests in `01 Project Plan.md`). Its old definition, kept for after the event:

- `firstrun run --targets targets.txt` runs 5 targets in parallel and prints one summary table.

## Three Demo Targets Come From Five Researched, and Three Show Real Drift

**The demo uses 3:** the neatlogs Python quickstart (#1), one real or fixture break (#3 Chroma, or #5 the OpenAI v0 fixture), and FirstRun's own README. Targets #2 and #4 stay as backups.

From `_agent-research/target-quickstarts.md`, checked 2026-10-08. Nobody ran these yet. Run them only after kickoff, through FirstRun.

| # | Target | Why it is in | Drift found by reading, not running |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | neatlogs Python SDK | Judge-related | The README uses `instrumentations=["openai"]` and the docs use `neatlogs.wrap(OpenAI())`. Open issue #172: `instrumentations=["langgraph"]` traces nothing. |
| 2 | Entire CLI on Linux | Judge-related | `install.sh` stops with "curl is required but not installed" on slim images, and the requirements list does not name curl. |
| 3 | Chroma | Popular | An error message links `docs.trychroma.com/deployment/migration`, which returns 404. |
| 4 | FastMCP | Popular | No drift found. A clean pass is a result too. |
| 5 | OpenAI v0 README, Wayback snapshot 20230802050711 | Known-broken fixture | `openai.ChatCompletion` was removed in SDK v1. Label it a fixture everywhere. |

**Backup for slot 5:** the Chroma usage guide, Wayback snapshot 20230521050959.

**Target 2 is the best ask-once demo.** Missing curl could be an environment issue, so the fix goes in the container, or a docs bug, so the requirements list gets fixed. FirstRun cannot be sure, so it asks you once. Show that moment in video beat 2.

**PR targets:** docs.neatlogs.com and docs.entire.io have no public docs repo. PRs for targets 1 and 2 go to `neatlogs/neatlogs` (README.MD) and `entireio/cli` (README.md, scripts/install.sh).

**Be kind to the judges' own products.** For targets 1 and 2, post the finding as a gift: open the issue or PR first, then thank the team in the post.

## Ten Things Are Out of Scope

Any idea below waits until after the event, whatever it is.

- A hosted web UI. The terminal and the neatlogs dashboard are the live UI. One static HTML report page is in scope (track T6, `22 Packaging and Distribution.md`).
- Scheduling nightly runs. Say "runs nightly" in the pitch only as the product plan, and show it in the cfo.ai model, not in code.
- Opening PRs automatically.
- Windows or macOS containers.
- Quickstarts that need a paid account.
- Multi-page tutorials longer than 10 steps.
- Video or screenshot steps in docs.
- Payments with Dodo.
- Crustdata enrichment.
- Any second product idea.

# FirstRun: The Agent That Does Your Quickstart Before Your Users Do

FirstRun reads a dev tool's quickstart page, runs every step in a clean container like a brand-new developer, and stops only when the last step works. When a step breaks, it finds the cause, patches the docs, proves the patch in a second clean run, and opens a pull request.

One line for the video: **"Your quickstart broke last Tuesday. Your users found out first. FirstRun finds out first now."**

## The Simple Version Wins, and Every Feature Must Pass Three Tests

The judges see about 100 projects. The one they remember can be said in one breath and shown in one minute. Every feature passes three tests, or it waits until after the event:

1. **Explain test.** It fits the one-sentence pitch below without a second sentence.
2. **Demo test.** It shows up on screen in the 60-second run below.
3. **Score test.** A judging category or an evidence item needs it.

**The pitch, one sentence:** "FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run."

**The whole product is one command:**

```bash
firstrun run https://docs.example.com/quickstart
```

**The output is one screen, three lines that matter:**

```text
✗ step 3/6  pip install chromadb==0.3   ->  No matching distribution
✓ fixed     docs bug: pin removed, patched step 3
✓ verified  fresh container, 6/6 steps pass, 94 s, $0.04
```

Those three lines are a design target, not a result. The numbers on them come from the real run on the day.

**The 60-second demo follows that order:** red step, the agent's reason, green verified, the drafted PR. Then one click into the neatlogs trace that shows the same run as spans.

**The three words of the story:** break, fix, prove. The video, the README and every post use these three words.

**Cut, because each fails at least one test:**

| Feature | Fails | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|
| Layer 3, the parallel coordinator | Explain test: it needs a second sentence | After the event |
| AWS nightly runner | Demo test: nothing visible in 60 seconds | Say "runs nightly" only as the product plan in cfo.ai |
| Crustdata owner lookup | Score test: no category needs it | After the event |
| A web UI or a static HTML report page | Demo test: the terminal plus neatlogs already show it | After the event, unless Chetan says the terminal confuses judges |
| 5 demo targets | Demo test: 3 tell the same story faster | Keep 3: the neatlogs quickstart, one real or fixture break, FirstRun's own README |

**The three tests never touch the required tools.** neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai are mandatory, so rule F5 in `07 Rules We Follow.md` protects every use of them. The tests cut FirstRun features only.

**Kept, because each passes all three:** the planner, the clean container, recovery with ask-once, the verification run, the drafted PR, neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints and Trails, and the cfo.ai plan.

**The Entire checkpoint-in-PR idea stays a stretch.** It passes the explain test only as "and every PR links the agent session that wrote it". Build it only after the 60-second demo works end to end.

## The Problem Is Silent Docs Rot

- A quickstart breaks when a package gets renamed, a flag gets removed or a version moves. Nobody on the team gets an alert.
- The first person who finds the break is a new user. Most new users leave instead of filing an issue.
- DevRel teams track "time to first success", but nobody measures it every night.

You run DevRel at AccuKnox. You write docs and quickstarts. This problem is yours, so the pitch is honest and you can talk about it without notes.

## Why This Idea Beats the Other Two

| Option | One-line verdict |
|---|---|
| **O1 FirstRun (pick this)** | Every judge works at a dev-tool company and owns docs or onboarding. Clear value, easy to demo, hits all 8 focus areas. |
| O2 Trace Medic: an agent that reads neatlogs traces of another agent and ships the fix | Maximum neatlogs use, but it copies neatlogs' own product. Many teams will build it. |
| O3 Claim Court: an agent that fact-checks a technical blog post with sources | Fits your writing system, but research agents are common and the demo is less visual. |

Your Jeff bookshelf cannot be the entry, because all code must be written during the event. Its Jev ranking idea lives on inside FirstRun as the failure classifier.

## The Last Winner Tested Docs Too, and FirstRun Must Look Different

At Syndicate by Maximor (Sep 5 to 6, co-hosted by neatlogs), Prateek Karnal and Ajay Yadav judged. First place went to **Skeptic**, an agent that tested its own tools' docs, found 12 of 12 documented promises broken, and published a corrected `TOOLS.md`. Second place, **Loop**, showed task success going from 0% to 100% across 3 runs.

This proves two judges reward docs testing. It also means FirstRun must look different from Skeptic in the first 15 seconds of the video:

- Skeptic tested the docs of the tools inside its own agent. FirstRun tests public quickstarts of real products, end to end, in a real container.
- Skeptic published a corrected file. FirstRun opens a PR on the real project.
- Copy what made both winners win: real before and after numbers, an honest null result when one happens, and one narrow problem.

Name Skeptic only if a judge asks. Show the difference instead of claiming it.

## How FirstRun Covers All 8 Focus Areas

The judges score "the agent" against these eight areas. FirstRun hits each one by design, not as an add-on.

| Focus area | What FirstRun does |
|---|---|
| Planning | Turns the docs page into an ordered runbook: each step, its command, and the result it expects. |
| Tool use | Firecrawl reads the docs. A shell runs inside a Docker container. GitHub opens the PR. |
| State | Writes a checkpoint after every step, so a crashed run resumes at the step it reached. |
| Context | Loads only the quickstart page and the pages it links to, never the whole docs site. |
| Execution | Keeps going until the last step passes or the retry budget runs out. |
| Recovery | On a failed step it classifies the cause, searches for the fix, patches, and retries. |
| Verification | Re-runs the patched runbook in a fresh container with no improvising allowed. Only a pass counts. |
| Iteration | Each step's real output decides the next action. |

## The Agent Asks a Human Once, Then Reuses the Answer

Ajay Yadav, the neatlogs founder, wrote "Self-healing is self-defeating" on 30 Sep. His fix is "ask just once": the agent asks a human on a new judgment call, saves the answer, and reuses it.

FirstRun builds that in. When it cannot tell whether a failure is a docs bug or intended behavior, it asks you once in the terminal. It stores your answer in `precedents.json` and never asks that question again. Jev makes the call and returns a probability, so FirstRun asks only when the probability sits below 0.7.

The FAQ says each tool needs "a clear role", and the video must cover all three.

| **cfo.ai** | Plans the business with real numbers. The cost per run comes from neatlogs, not from a guess. | A read-only cfo.ai Page link plus the `.xlsx` export, with pricing, costs, revenue and runway. |

## The Stack Uses Python and Your Own Tools

- **Language:** Python, because neatlogs auto-instruments Python and TypeScript has no auto-instrumentation.
- **Agent:** Claude Agent SDK (Python). neatlogs turns each `query()` into an AGENT span, with one LLM span per turn and one TOOL span per tool call.

Read `D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\jev\jev.py` for the API shape, but do not copy the file, because all code must be new. It classifies each failure as docs bug, environment, product bug or needs a secret, with a probability.

## The Scope Is Three Layers, and Only Layer 1 Is Mandatory

Build in this order. Stop adding layers at 2:00 PM IST on Monday, whatever is done.

1. **Layer 1, must ship (Saturday):** one quickstart URL in, a runbook out, every step run in Docker, a report out, every run traced in neatlogs.

3. **Layer 3, nice to have (Sunday night):** a coordinator that runs 5 quickstarts in parallel, one worker each, then merges the reports. Prateek Karnal builds parallel agent fleets, so he will notice this.

## Five Test Quickstarts Follow Four Rules

Pick them on Friday. Picking is planning, so it is allowed before kickoff.

# FirstRun Spec

This spec is planning, written in prose before kickoff, as the rules allow. It holds no code. At kickoff, Claude Code builds from it through the prompts in `05 Kickoff Prompts.md`. Every decision here is made once, so Saturday goes to building.

## FirstRun Takes One URL and Returns a Verdict With Proof

- **Input:** the URL of a quickstart page, or a file `targets.txt` with one URL per line.
- **Output per run**, in `runs/<run_id>/`:
  - `report.md`: pass or fail, the first failed step, the cause, the fix, time to first success, cost.
  - `runbook.json`: the steps as the planner read them.
  - `state.json`: the checkpoint after each step.
  - `patch.diff`: the docs change, only when a docs bug was found and verified.
  - `pr_body.md`: a draft PR text, only with a verified patch.
- **The user:** a DevRel or docs engineer who wants to know their quickstart works before a new user tries it.

## The Command Line Has Four Commands

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `firstrun run <url>` | One full run on one quickstart |
| `firstrun run --targets targets.txt` | One run per line, one after another. |
| `firstrun run <url> --resume <run_id>` | Continue a crashed run from the last good step |
| `firstrun report` | A summary table across every run in `runs/` |

## A Runbook Step Has Six Fields

The planner turns the docs page into a list of steps. Each step has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | Step number, starting at 1 |
| `intent` | One plain sentence: what this step is for, such as "install the SDK" |
| `command` | The exact shell command from the docs, unchanged |
| `files` | Files the docs tell the user to create, with their content |
| `expected` | What success looks like: exit code 0, a line of output, a file that exists |
| `source_line` | Where in the docs page this step came from, so a patch can point at it |

The planner copies commands exactly. It never fixes a command while planning. Fixing happens only in recovery, where it is logged.

## The Model Is Fixed at Sonnet 5.5, Medium Effort

- Every model call in FirstRun uses `claude-sonnet-5-5` at medium effort. One constant sets both, and no other file names a model.
- Auth is `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, so calls draw on the Claude subscription. There is no Anthropic API key, and AWS Bedrock is not available on the hackathon account.
- Jev handles failure classification and is not an Anthropic call.
- Cost per run is the token count from neatlogs times the Sonnet 5.5 list price. Every report and the cfo.ai plan label it "list price, not billed".

## Each Step Moves Through Six States

`pending` → `running` → `passed`, or `running` → `failed` → `recovering` → `passed` (with a patch) or `gave_up`.

After the last step, the whole run moves to `verifying`, then to `verified` or `unverified`.

## Four Failure Classes Decide the Next Action

When a step fails, Jev classifies the error output into one class and returns a probability for each class.

| Class | Example | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| `docs_bug` | Package renamed, flag removed, wrong import path | Search for the fix, patch the step, retry |
| `environment` | Missing system package in the base image, network timeout | Fix the container, not the docs. Retry. Do not count it as a docs bug. |
| `product_bug` | The tool itself crashes on a correct command | Stop. Report it as a product bug. No docs patch. |
| `needs_secret` | The step asks for an API key the container lacks | Use a test key from the allowlist if one exists. Otherwise stop and report. |

**Ask once.** If the top probability is below 0.7, FirstRun asks the user in the terminal: "Is this a docs bug, an environment issue, a product bug, or a missing secret?" It stores the answer in `precedents.json`, keyed by a short signature of the error, and reuses it without asking again.

## Recovery Has a Hard Budget

The budget protects against the agent looping, which is the most common agent failure the neatlogs judges look for.

| Limit | Value | When it trips |
|---|---|---|
| Attempts per step | 3 | The step is marked `gave_up` |
| Tool calls per run | 25 | The run stops and reports |
| Cost per run | $0.50 | The run stops and reports |
| Time per step | 5 minutes | The command is killed |

Each limit check is a `GUARDRAIL` span in neatlogs, so a tripped limit is visible in the trace.

## Verification Allows No Improvising

A run counts as `verified` only when all three are true:

1. A brand-new container runs the runbook with every patch applied.
2. No model call happens during the verification run. Only the stored commands run.
3. Every step meets its `expected` result.

Verification is what turns "the agent says it works" into "it works". Say that sentence in the video.

## Neatlogs Sees Every Part of a Run

| Part of FirstRun | Span kind | Span name |
|---|---|---|
| One whole run | `WORKFLOW` | `firstrun.run` |
| Reading the docs page | `TOOL` | `read_docs` |
| Planning the runbook | `AGENT` | `planner` |
| Running one step | `TOOL` | `step.<id>` |
| Classifying a failure | `TOOL` | `classify_failure` |
| Recovery for one step | `AGENT` | `recover.<id>` |
| A budget check | `GUARDRAIL` | `budget` |
| The verification run | `GUARDRAIL` | `verify` |

**Tags:** `v1` for the first version, `v2` after the fix. **Metadata on every run:** `target` (the tool name), `run_id`, `variant`.

**Detections to create on Sunday morning,** in the neatlogs dashboard:

1. Condition: `tool_call_count > 25`, which catches a looping agent.
2. Condition: `cost_usd > 0.50`, which catches a run over budget.
3. Regex on step output: `command not found|No module named|unrecognized arguments`, which catches the most common docs breaks.

**Eval:** one human eval question per run, "Is the docs patch correct?", plus one AI evaluator that scores whether `report.md` names the real failed step. Paid plans are free during neatHack, so the AI evaluator costs nothing.

## The Container Is the Safety Boundary

- One fresh container per run, removed after the run.
- No folder from your PC is mounted into the container.
- Network access stays on, because quickstarts install packages.
- The only secrets in the container are test keys from an allowlist file that never enters git.
- FirstRun never opens a PR on another project by itself. It writes `pr_body.md`, and you open the PR by hand after you read it.

## Each Layer Has a Definition of Done

**Layer 1 is done when:**

- `firstrun run <neatlogs quickstart URL>` finishes and writes `report.md`.
- The run shows in neatlogs as one trace, with a `TOOL` span per step.
- A test with a saved docs page passes with no network.

**Layer 2 is done when:**

- A known-broken fixture fails on a step, gets classified, gets patched, and ends `verified`.
- A second run with the same error asks no question, because the precedent exists.
- `patch.diff` and `pr_body.md` exist for the fixture.

**Layer 3 is cut** (see the three tests in `01 Project Plan.md`). Its old definition, kept for after the event:

- `firstrun run --targets targets.txt` runs 5 targets in parallel and prints one summary table.

## Three Demo Targets Come From Five Researched, and Three Show Real Drift

**The demo uses 3:** the neatlogs Python quickstart (#1), one real or fixture break (#3 Chroma, or #5 the OpenAI v0 fixture), and FirstRun's own README. Targets #2 and #4 stay as backups.

From `_agent-research/target-quickstarts.md`, checked 2026-10-08. Nobody ran these yet. Run them only after kickoff, through FirstRun.

| # | Target | Why it is in | Drift found by reading, not running |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | neatlogs Python SDK | Judge-related | The README uses `instrumentations=["openai"]` and the docs use `neatlogs.wrap(OpenAI())`. Open issue #172: `instrumentations=["langgraph"]` traces nothing. |
| 2 | Entire CLI on Linux | Judge-related | `install.sh` stops with "curl is required but not installed" on slim images, and the requirements list does not name curl. |
| 3 | Chroma | Popular | An error message links `docs.trychroma.com/deployment/migration`, which returns 404. |
| 4 | FastMCP | Popular | No drift found. A clean pass is a result too. |
| 5 | OpenAI v0 README, Wayback snapshot 20230802050711 | Known-broken fixture | `openai.ChatCompletion` was removed in SDK v1. Label it a fixture everywhere. |

**Backup for slot 5:** the Chroma usage guide, Wayback snapshot 20230521050959.

**Target 2 is the best ask-once demo.** Missing curl could be an environment issue, so the fix goes in the container, or a docs bug, so the requirements list gets fixed. FirstRun cannot be sure, so it asks you once. Show that moment in video beat 2.

**PR targets:** docs.neatlogs.com and docs.entire.io have no public docs repo. PRs for targets 1 and 2 go to `neatlogs/neatlogs` (README.MD) and `entireio/cli` (README.md, scripts/install.sh).

**Be kind to the judges' own products.** For targets 1 and 2, post the finding as a gift: open the issue or PR first, then thank the team in the post.

## Ten Things Are Out of Scope

Any idea below waits until after the event, whatever it is.

- A hosted web UI. The terminal and the neatlogs dashboard are the live UI. One static HTML report page is in scope (track T6, `22 Packaging and Distribution.md`).
- Scheduling nightly runs. Say "runs nightly" in the pitch only as the product plan, and show it in the cfo.ai model, not in code.
- Opening PRs automatically.
- Windows or macOS containers.
- Quickstarts that need a paid account.
- Multi-page tutorials longer than 10 steps.
- Video or screenshot steps in docs.
- Payments with Dodo.
- Crustdata enrichment.
- Any second product idea.

# Paste These Prompts Into Claude Code, One at a Time

Use them only after kickoff, Sat Oct 10, 12:30 PM IST. Open Claude Code inside the new `firstrun` repo, not inside the vault. Paste one prompt, wait until it is done, check the result, then paste the next.

```powershell
cmd /c mklink /J plan "D:\Atharva\NOTES\PROJECTS\NeatHack - 10 October"
```

```bash
entire status
```



## Prompt 1 Creates the Repo and the Build Log

```text
We are building FirstRun for the neatHack hackathon (rules: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon).
FirstRun is a Python agent. Input: the URL of a dev tool's quickstart page. It reads the
page, turns it into an ordered runbook of steps (command, expected result), runs each step
inside a fresh Docker container (Docker runs in WSL: call it as `wsl -d Ubuntu-22.04 docker ...`),
and writes a report of which step failed and why.

Model access: the Claude Agent SDK authenticates with CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, read from
D:\Atharva\NOTES\.env at run time. There is no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Load the env file in code, never copy
the value into the repo. Tested 2026-10-10: a query() returned a result with only that token set.

The full spec is plan/08 FirstRun Spec.md. Read it now. Every later prompt builds against it,
including the span names, the failure classes, the budget and the definition of done.
plan/ is a private folder and is in .gitignore. Never commit it and never copy text from it
into the public repo.

Do this now, nothing more:
1. Install the neatHack build skill from https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/skill and create
   hackathon.md at the repo root following it.
2. Create a Python 3.11 project with `py -3.11 -m venv .venv`: pyproject.toml, src/firstrun/,
   tests/, README.md stub. Keep the existing .gitignore.
3. Add neatlogs: pip install -U "neatlogs[anthropic]" and the Claude Agent SDK. Initialize
   neatlogs with workflow_name="firstrun", debug=True, capture_logs=True, key from
   NEATLOGS_API_KEY. Prove one trace arrives with a hello-world span.
4. Run `entire status` and `entire checkpoint list` yourself and paste the output into
   hackathon.md, so the build log shows Entire is on from the first commit.
5. Set up Entire Graph and, if Trails access is granted, Trails. Run these yourself:
   `entire plugin install graph`, `entire graph init-agents --repo .`, and
   `entire runner setup -y` (Trails only). Commit the generated .entire/ files,
   AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.
6. Commit with a clear message. Then stop and show me the neatlogs trace URL.
```

## Prompt 2 Builds the Runbook Planner

```text
Build the planner. Use the firecrawl CLI (`firecrawl scrape <url> --format markdown`) to
read the quickstart page. Load only that page, plus pages it links to that a step needs.

command, files to create, and expected_result. Validate the JSON with pydantic.
```

```text
Build the executor. For each runbook step, run the command inside one fresh Docker
container per run (python:3.11-slim unless the runbook says otherwise), capture stdout,
```

```text
Tag runs tags=["v2"]. Commit after each numbered item.
```

Layer 3 fails the explain test in `01 Project Plan.md`. Do not paste it. It stays here only for after the event.

```text
Add a coordinator: it takes targets.txt, starts one worker per URL in parallel
```

```text
5. Then run FirstRun on its own README and paste the result at the top of the README.
Commit and push.
```

```text
- Any front end you build (landing page, report page) runs the impeccable skill and follows
  plan/28 Packaging Design Spec.md: Apple style, light mode, real logos, one action per screen.

NEATLOGS RULES (from the official setup guide, checked 2026-10-10)
- NEATLOGS_API_KEY is already in this session's environment. It is the project API key, not an
  nlw_ HTTP key. Use the SDK with it. Never print it.
- The neatlogs CLI profile "work" is signed in. Run it as
  `npx --yes -p node@22 -p neatlogs-cli@0.2.0 -- neatlogs ...`. A trace readback worked on 2026-10-10.

- Do kickoff prompt 1 in full. Commit. Prove one neatlogs trace.

STEP 2, CONTRACTS (you, alone, one commit)
- Write src/firstrun/models.py with pydantic models for the six runbook fields, StepResult,
  RunState, the six step states, the four failure classes, Patch and Budget. Names and fields
  come from plan/08. Write one stub per module with the exact function signature the table
  below names and a docstring only. Tests import the stubs. Commit. Workers build against
  this commit, so nothing else may change models.py after it without telling the lead.

STEP 3, FAN OUT (one message, six workers T1 to T6 in parallel, each with isolation: "worktree")
Give each worker: its track text below, the path plan/08, and the rule "touch only your files,
commit on your branch, run your tests, report the commit SHA and test output in 5 lines".

STEP 4, MERGE (you)
- Merge branches in order T3, T1, T2, T4, T5, T6. Run the full test suite after each merge.
  Then start T7 as a worker: it turns every row of plan/23 into a test and fixes what fails.
  Fix conflicts yourself. Run `entire status` and `entire checkpoint list`, and put the output
  in hackathon.md.
- Push main. Then run `firstrun run --targets targets.txt` with tags=["v1"]. Save the traces.
- Run the official neatlogs check (prompt 3b, text in plan/_agent-research/neatlogs-agent-prompt.md).
- Tick the Saturday row of the F5 table in plan/07. Write the v1 mistakes list to plan/20 Build Log.md.
- At the end of every block, tick plan/21 and run the seven quiet-gap checks in it.

STEP 5, SUNDAY AND MONDAY
- Follow plan/09 Run Sheet for Sunday and Monday. Use prompts 4 and 7. Use workers again
  wherever two tasks touch different files.
- Stop and ask Atharva only for: a detection created in the neatlogs dashboard, the ask-once
  answer, a PR to another project, the X submission. Everything else you decide and log.
```

## Seven Worker Tracks Split the Build by File

T1 to T6 start from the contracts commit. T7 starts after the merge. Each track owns separate files, so the merges stay clean.

| Track | Builds | Owns | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 Planner | `read_docs` (Firecrawl scrape) and the `planner` agent, which returns a validated runbook. Spans per plan/08. | `planner.py`, `tests/test_planner.py` | A saved markdown fixture produces a valid runbook with no network. |
| T2 Executor | One fresh container per run through `wsl -d Ubuntu-22.04 docker`. One `step.<id>` span per step. `state.json` after each step. `--resume`. `report.md`. The `firstrun run` and `firstrun report` commands. | `executor.py`, `state.py`, `report.py`, `cli.py`, `tests/test_executor.py` | A two-step runbook runs in a container and resumes after a forced crash. |

A second run asks no question. |

Built on sample runs in its own fixtures. | `report_html.py`, `report/template.html`, tests | The page renders from sample data, shows "missing" for absent values, and prints its build time. |

| Module | Function | Takes | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `planner` | `plan(url)` | Docs URL | `Runbook` |
| `executor` | `run_step(container, step)` | Container handle, `Step` | `StepResult` |
| `executor` | `run(runbook, run_id, resume)` | `Runbook` | `RunState` |

# Entire Playbook for neatHack

Source: https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/, saved in full at `_agent-research/entire-guide.md`. A rescrape on 2026-10-10 at about 10:00 IST found no change since the morning.

Entire counts twice. It is one of the three required tools in the 25% category. It also has its own prize, **Best Use of Entire**, for "the most creative use of Checkpoints, Graph or Brain". Haimantika Mitra runs it (hmitra@entire.io), and she is also a main judge.

## Five Setup Steps Come From the Page

| # | Step | Command or place | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sign in with GitHub and install the Entire GitHub App | https://entire.io | ⏳ yours. Syncing a repo takes up to an hour. |
| 2 | Install the CLI and log in | `entire login` | ✅ logged in, 29 days |
| 3 | Enable Entire in the repo before the first commit | `entire enable --agent claude-code --search-skill --agent-help-skill` | At 12:30 IST. The page shows `--agent codex`, and `claude-code` is our agent. |
| 4 | Turn on Trails | After kickoff, in the repo on entire.io: **Settings → General**, turn on Runners, Auto build on push and Trails. Then `entire runner setup -y`, commit and push `.entire/`, then `entire trail create`. Each Trail is backed by a GitHub PR. | ✅ access enabled by Haimantika Mitra on 2026-10-10 |
| 5 | Install Graph and Brain | `entire plugin install graph`, `entire graph init-agents --repo .`, then the Brain script and `entire brain setup`, `entire brain init-agents` | Prompt 1 after kickoff |

The page's own check that Graph works: the agent's first move is `entire-graph search` instead of a grep.

**Brain on Windows:** the install script is bash, and its watcher service runs only on macOS and Linux. Run the script in Git Bash, then use `entire brain setup --no-daemon`. Earlier research on 2026-10-08 found this flag in the entire-brain README.

## Use All Four Features, Each With a Visible Proof

| Feature | How FirstRun uses it | The proof for judges |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpoints | Every commit from commit 1 carries the Claude Code session behind it | The entire.io commit view, with **Sessions** then **Changes** |
| Trails | One Trail per build layer: Layer 1, then Layer 2. Runners evaluate every push. | The Trail page with Runner findings |
| Graph | The build agent searches the repo through the graph | `entire graph stats --repo .` gives the tokens saved. Put that number in the README and the video. |
| Brain | Sunday's session picks up Saturday's decisions with no re-explaining | Show Brain answering "why does recovery stop at 3 attempts?" with the Saturday session as the source |

## One Idea Aims at the Best Use of Entire Prize

**Every docs PR FirstRun drafts carries an Entire checkpoint of the agent session that wrote the fix.**

- A docs maintainer who gets a PR from an agent asks one question: why should I trust this change? The checkpoint answers it with the full session: the failed step, the error, the search, the patch and the clean re-run.
- It matches two ideas on Entire's own list: "a reviewer that checks intent" and "a checkpoint-to-demo generator".
- It matches Haimantika's post of Oct 6, "Sharing Sessions is the New Social Coding", where she shares Codex sessions through checkpoints so reviewers see the prompts.

**How it could work, unverified until kickoff:** the Claude Agent SDK runs the same `claude` CLI that Entire hooks into. If FirstRun runs its fix step with Claude Code inside a clone of the docs repo where Entire is enabled, Entire may record that session as a checkpoint. Then `pr_body.md` gets a line: "Agent session behind this fix: https://entire.io/gh/OWNER/REPO/commit/SHA".

**Test it Sunday, after Layer 2 works.** It is a stretch goal. If the test fails in 45 minutes, drop it and keep the four features above.

## Submit With These Five Items

From the page's checklist:

1. **Project:** the name and a short explanation.
2. **Entire usage:** which features, and how each one supports FirstRun. Use the table above.
3. **Demo:** a working link or a short recording of the main workflow.
4. **Repository:** source code with setup and run instructions.
5. **Checkpoint:** an accessible link plus its checkpoint ID, in the form `https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/commit/FULL_COMMIT_SHA`.

Before you submit:

1. Run `entire status` and confirm every checkpoint is synced.
2. Open the repo on entire.io, then the branch, the commit and the checkpoint.
3. Check that **Sessions** and **Changes** both open in a logged-out window. The repo is public, so its checkpoints are public too.

## Seven Links Cover the Rest

- Quickstart: https://docs.entire.io/quickstart
- Checkpoints: https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/capture-checkpoints
- Graph: https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/set-up-graph
- Search: https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-in-cli
- Brain reference: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/blob/main/docs/reference.md#how-agents-use-the-brain
- Agent integration protocol: https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/build-an-agent-integration
- Entire Discord: https://discord.gg/tjhUTA7J7

# Grading Checklist and Judge Map

Sources: `_agent-research/hackathon-rules-verbatim.md` for the rubric, `02 Judges and Mentors.md` for the people. The lead agent ticks this file at the end of every block. Atharva reads only the "Gaps" column.

## Five Categories Carry 100 Points, and Each One Has a Proof File

| Category | Weight | What earns it | Proof file or link | Owner | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The agent | 30% | All 8 focus areas visible in one run (table below) | `runs/*/report.md`, trace links | Lead | [ ] |
| neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai | 25% | A clear role for each, covered in the video | `evidence/`, README sections | Lead | [ ] |
| Demo video | 20% | 3 minutes or less, 5 points for each tool | YouTube link | Vault chat | [ ] |
| Building in public | 15% | 5 or more posts tagged #neatHack, with failures and numbers | Post URLs in `hackathon.md` | Vault chat | [ ] |
| Usefulness and originality | 10% | A real docs team would run it nightly | README pitch, the PRs and issues opened | Lead | [ ] |

## Eight Focus Areas Each Map to One Feature a Judge Can See

| Focus area | FirstRun feature | Where the judge sees it |
|---|---|---|
| Planning | `planner` turns the docs page into a runbook | `runbook.json`, the `planner` span |
| Tool use | Firecrawl read, Docker run, Jev classify | One `TOOL` span per call |
| State | `state.json` after every step | `--resume` works after a forced crash |
| Context | Only the quickstart page and the pages a step needs | Token count per run in neatlogs |
| Execution | One fresh container per run | `step.<id>` spans with exit codes |
| Recovery | Classify, search, patch, retry, 3 attempts | A trace with a failed step and the retry |
| Verification | A model-free re-run in a new container | The `verify` span, status `verified` |
| Iteration | v1 traces, a detection, an Investigate, v2 traces | The before and after table |

## Seven Claims Need Proof, and the Checklist Names the File

- [ ] **Agent improved:** two neatlogs traces, v1 and v2, with the numbers table in the README. Real numbers only.
- [ ] **neatlogs used:** trace links in `evidence/neatlogs.md`, plus 2 detections, 1 Investigate and 1 eval.
- [ ] **Entire used:** `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer on every commit, the entire.io commit link with the full SHA, `evidence/graph.ndjson`, and the jury self-test output.
- [ ] **cfo.ai used:** the share link, `business/plan.xlsx` and `BUSINESS_PLAN.md`, with price, costs, revenue and runway.
- [ ] **Recovery shown:** one exported failed-and-recovered trace in `evidence/`.
- [ ] **Built in public:** every post URL with #neatHack in `hackathon.md`.
- [ ] **Code written during the event:** the first commit is after 2026-10-10 12:30 IST, and `hackathon.md` says planning happened before in a private repo.

## What Each Judge Will Look for, and the Artifact That Answers Them

| Judge | Role | Looks for | Artifact that answers it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Haimantika Mitra | Docs at Entire | Entire on from commit 1. A README a developer can reproduce in minutes. | First commit carries a checkpoint. README has a 5-minute quickstart. |
| Abhi Singh | Solutions engineer at Entire | A clean install, real tests, cost numbers. | `pip install` then `firstrun run` works on a clean machine. `pytest` passes. Cost per run in the README. |
| Prateek Karnal | Parallel agents | Parallel work, measured numbers, an honest failure log. | The build used 5 parallel worker agents. The README carries a "what broke" section with numbers. |
| Ajay Yadav | neatlogs founder | A failure traced, fixed and proven fixed. A human asked only at the real call. | The ask-once store. A verified fix. No fully self-fixing loop. |
| Akshay Hangloo | neatlogs product | An agent that catches its own quality drop. Evals on real runs. A polished UI. | 2 detections, the AI evaluator, the static report page (T6). |

## Five Mentors Add Questions, and Each One Gets a Short Answer Ready

| Mentor | Probable question | Answer to have ready |
|---|---|---|
| Chetan Raj | Where does a judge stop trusting a demo? | The video shows a real run from terminal to trace, with no cuts inside the run. |
| Rohan Mukherjee | Can the agent game its own verification? | No. Verification calls no model and runs only the stored commands in a new container. |
| Rithvik K | What if the run crashes halfway? | `state.json` after each step and `--resume`. |
| Ankush Dharkar | What is the smallest human check? | One question, asked once, stored as a precedent. |
| Karan Pargal | What do the first 30 seconds show? | One broken step in red, then the agent finding it. |

## The Community Award Looks at Genuine Interest, so Three Things Count

1. **Quality of the launch.** One post a day with a failure and a number in it.
2. **Gifts to the judges' own products.** An issue or a PR for neatlogs and Entire, opened by hand, then a thank-you post.
3. **Replies to every comment in the first 24 hours.** Never buy likes. Bots disqualify the entry.

## Seven Gaps Lose Points Quietly, so the Lead Checks Them Every Night

1. A tool with no use that day (rule F5).
2. A video beat that names fewer than 5 points for a tool.
3. A post with no number or no failure in it.
4. A trace link that needs a login. Check logged out.
5. A commit with no `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer.
6. A cfo.ai number that did not come from neatlogs.
7. A claim in the README with no proof file.

## Submit Between 7:00 and 7:05 PM on Monday

The F4 controls live in `07 Rules We Follow.md`. This file adds one check: before clicking, tick all seven claims above. If one is open, submit anyway, and finish it before 11:55 PM in the repo.

# Grading Checklist and Judge Map

Sources: `_agent-research/hackathon-rules-verbatim.md` for the rubric, `02 Judges and Mentors.md` for the people. The lead agent ticks this file at the end of every block. Atharva reads only the "Gaps" column.

## Five Categories Carry 100 Points, and Each One Has a Proof File

| Category | Weight | What earns it | Proof file or link | Owner | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The agent | 30% | All 8 focus areas visible in one run (table below) | `runs/*/report.md`, trace links | Lead | [ ] |
| neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai | 25% | A clear role for each, covered in the video | `evidence/`, README sections | Lead | [ ] |
| Demo video | 20% | 3 minutes or less, 5 points for each tool | YouTube link | Vault chat | [ ] |
| Building in public | 15% | 5 or more posts tagged #neatHack, with failures and numbers | Post URLs in `hackathon.md` | Vault chat | [ ] |
| Usefulness and originality | 10% | A real docs team would run it nightly | README pitch, the PRs and issues opened | Lead | [ ] |

## Eight Focus Areas Each Map to One Feature a Judge Can See

| Focus area | FirstRun feature | Where the judge sees it |
|---|---|---|
| Planning | `planner` turns the docs page into a runbook | `runbook.json`, the `planner` span |
| Tool use | Firecrawl read, Docker run, Jev classify | One `TOOL` span per call |
| State | `state.json` after every step | `--resume` works after a forced crash |
| Context | Only the quickstart page and the pages a step needs | Token count per run in neatlogs |
| Execution | One fresh container per run | `step.<id>` spans with exit codes |
| Recovery | Classify, search, patch, retry, 3 attempts | A trace with a failed step and the retry |
| Verification | A model-free re-run in a new container | The `verify` span, status `verified` |
| Iteration | v1 traces, a detection, an Investigate, v2 traces | The before and after table |

## Seven Claims Need Proof, and the Checklist Names the File

- [ ] **Agent improved:** two neatlogs traces, v1 and v2, with the numbers table in the README. Real numbers only.
- [ ] **neatlogs used:** trace links in `evidence/neatlogs.md`, plus 2 detections, 1 Investigate and 1 eval.
- [ ] **Entire used:** `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer on every commit, the entire.io commit link with the full SHA, `evidence/graph.ndjson`, and the jury self-test output.
- [ ] **cfo.ai used:** the share link, `business/plan.xlsx` and `BUSINESS_PLAN.md`, with price, costs, revenue and runway.
- [ ] **Recovery shown:** one exported failed-and-recovered trace in `evidence/`.
- [ ] **Built in public:** every post URL with #neatHack in `hackathon.md`.
- [ ] **Code written during the event:** the first commit is after 2026-10-10 12:30 IST, and `hackathon.md` says planning happened before in a private repo.

## What Each Judge Will Look for, and the Artifact That Answers Them

| Judge | Role | Looks for | Artifact that answers it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Haimantika Mitra | Docs at Entire | Entire on from commit 1. A README a developer can reproduce in minutes. | First commit carries a checkpoint. README has a 5-minute quickstart. |
| Abhi Singh | Solutions engineer at Entire | A clean install, real tests, cost numbers. | `pip install` then `firstrun run` works on a clean machine. `pytest` passes. Cost per run in the README. |
| Prateek Karnal | Parallel agents | Parallel work, measured numbers, an honest failure log. | The build used 5 parallel worker agents. The README carries a "what broke" section with numbers. |
| Ajay Yadav | neatlogs founder | A failure traced, fixed and proven fixed. A human asked only at the real call. | The ask-once store. A verified fix. No fully self-fixing loop. |
| Akshay Hangloo | neatlogs product | An agent that catches its own quality drop. Evals on real runs. A polished UI. | 2 detections, the AI evaluator, the static report page (T6). |

## Five Mentors Add Questions, and Each One Gets a Short Answer Ready

| Mentor | Probable question | Answer to have ready |
|---|---|---|
| Chetan Raj | Where does a judge stop trusting a demo? | The video shows a real run from terminal to trace, with no cuts inside the run. |
| Rohan Mukherjee | Can the agent game its own verification? | No. Verification calls no model and runs only the stored commands in a new container. |
| Rithvik K | What if the run crashes halfway? | `state.json` after each step and `--resume`. |
| Ankush Dharkar | What is the smallest human check? | One question, asked once, stored as a precedent. |
| Karan Pargal | What do the first 30 seconds show? | One broken step in red, then the agent finding it. |

## The Community Award Looks at Genuine Interest, so Three Things Count

1. **Quality of the launch.** One post a day with a failure and a number in it.
2. **Gifts to the judges' own products.** An issue or a PR for neatlogs and Entire, opened by hand, then a thank-you post.
3. **Replies to every comment in the first 24 hours.** Never buy likes. Bots disqualify the entry.

## Seven Gaps Lose Points Quietly, so the Lead Checks Them Every Night

1. A tool with no use that day (rule F5).
2. A video beat that names fewer than 5 points for a tool.
3. A post with no number or no failure in it.
4. A trace link that needs a login. Check logged out.
5. A commit with no `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer.
6. A cfo.ai number that did not come from neatlogs.
7. A claim in the README with no proof file.

## Submit Between 7:00 and 7:05 PM on Monday

The F4 controls live in `07 Rules We Follow.md`. This file adds one check: before clicking, tick all seven claims above. If one is open, submit anyway, and finish it before 11:55 PM in the repo.

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using Glob, Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.
